newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai exports outlook still seen bleak near-term.
newsitem.headline: Thai exports outlook still seen bleak near-term.

text.p: The near-term outlook for Thai export growth remains bleak due to ongoing cyclical and structural adjustments for the sector and a likely loss of some U.S. trade privileges, analysts said on Monday.
An expected hike in U.S. interest rates, which would push up already high local rates, could drive up production costs and make the country's products more expensive, they told Reuters.

The export sector has been Thailand's major engine for growth in recent years. But last year's export performance was disastrous and the worst since 1983 as growth contracted 0.2 percent from a heady 23 percent increase posted in 1995.

The outlook for the sector is coloured by the possibility that Thailand could lose some of its U.S. General System of Preference (GSP) privileges. The privileges would be removed for products which accounted for more than 50 percent of market share in the United States or exceeded $75 million in annual sales value.

Thai exports that were "almost certain" to have GSP privileges removed this year included silver jewellery, microwave ovens and galvanised rubber gloves, according to Commerce Ministry officials. Those also likely to have the privilege revoked included ski and snowmobile gloves, hand-held CB transceivers and circuit panels.
These exports earned more than $400 million last year.

"Normally if a country loses privileges when it comes from a position of strength, like Singapore or Malaysia, the impact will be minimal," said Song Seng Wun, regional economist for HG Asia. "But with Thailand, the impact could be stronger, especially with the industries which are facing structural difficulties because the economy is slowing," he said.
Analysts said any significant export turnaround, which would be spurred mostly by a return of demand for electronics-related products, might not be seen until the second half of 1997.

"Thailand should not expect any significant impetus from exports this year as the ongoing structural transformation of the exports profile will continue to test the management capabilities of a coalition government yet to prove itself," Asia Equity research said in a report.

Khanchit Assavasamran of Vickers Ballas said the outlook of Thai electronics-related exports depended greatly on Singapore's market which has, in recent years, has absorbed almost half of Thailand's exports of computers and parts.
"Singapore's export data for January was rather disappointing. Unless its electronics exports pick up, any improvement on our sector will be limited," he said.
Singapore's non-oil domestic exports have suffered this year from sluggish demand for computer and electronic components.
The Commerce Ministry has forecast that Thai export growth this year will pick up and record nominal growth of 10 percent. The Bank of Thailand has forecast 7.7 percent growth.
Analysts said the expectations were ambitious but attainable as the 1996 base was very low.

Thailand had been too slow switching its exports focus to value-added and high-technology products in the past, and its recent scramble to do so meant the country's grip on markets for lower-end products was slipping, the analysts said.
Lower-cost producers such as China, Vietnam and Indonesia would overtake traditional low-end Thai items such as textiles and footwear, they added.
But a switch to high-technology production would cause the nation's import bill to swell because of the need to import raw materials and intermediate goods, analysts said.
